reaching.q: Explain what is meant by terminal velocity.
reaching.a: The constant speed reached when air resistance equals weight, so the resultant force is zero.

reaching.q: A 70 kg skydiver has a weight of 700 N. Calculate her acceleration at the instant she jumps.
Explain why the skydiver slows down when the parachute opens.
reaching.a: The parachute increases air resistance so it is now bigger than her weight. The resultant force acts upwards, so she decelerates.

mastering.q: A skydiver reaches terminal velocity, opens her parachute, then reaches a second, lower terminal velocity. Explain the changes in the forces acting on her throughout the whole descent, and describe how her acceleration changes at each stage.
mastering.a: At first weight is much greater than drag, so there is a large downward resultant force and she accelerates. As speed rises, drag rises until it equals weight. The resultant force is now zero and she falls at a constant terminal velocity. Opening the parachute causes a sudden large increase in drag, which now exceeds weight, so the resultant force acts upwards and she decelerates. As she slows, drag falls again until it once more equals weight, giving a second, lower terminal velocity.

When the line goes flat, the reaction has stopped completely.

build.intro: You will measure how the concentration of acid affects the volume of gas produced in one minute.

mastering.q: One group recorded 44 cm^3 at 0.5 mol/dm^3. Explain whether this is an anomaly.

mastering.q: Explain why doubling the concentration roughly doubles the volume of gas made in 60 s.
mastering.a: Doubling the concentration doubles the number of acid particles in the same volume, so collisions with the marble are twice as frequent and the reaction runs twice as fast.

build.question: Explain, in terms of particles, why increasing the temperature increases the rate of a reaction.
build.instruction: Mark each answer against the scheme. Give it a level and a mark out of 6.

levelDescriptors.desc: Clear explanation linking temperature to both collision frequency and collision energy, with reference to activation energy.
Links temperature to particle speed and to either frequency or energy of collisions, but not both.

samples.label: Student A
samples.text: The particles move faster when its hotter so they hit each other more. This makes the reaction go quicker.

developing.q: State the unit of rate when gas volume is measured.
Name the four factors that affect rate.
What is activation energy?
developing.a: The minimum energy needed for a collision to be successful.

reaching.q: Rewrite this answer to earn the mark: 'It goes faster because it is hot.'
reaching.a: The particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so collisions are more frequent and more of them exceed the activation energy.

reaching.q: 60 cm^3 of gas is made in 25 s. Calculate the mean rate.
Explain why a catalyst increases the rate.
reaching.a: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

mastering.q: Explain fully why surface area and temperature both increase rate, but for different reasons.
mastering.a: Surface area increases the number of exposed particles, so collisions are more frequent. The energy of each collision is unchanged. Temperature increases both the frequency of collisions and the energy of each one, so a greater proportion exceed the activation energy.

mastering.q: A student divided time by volume. Explain the error and give the correct working.

mastering.q: Explain why a rate graph plateaus at the same height regardless of temperature.
mastering.a: The plateau height depends on the amount of reactant, which is unchanged. Temperature only changes how quickly that amount is used up.

questions.q: What is the active site?
questions.a: The part of the enzyme where the substrate binds.

questions.a: Its active site is a complementary shape to only one substrate.

developing.q: Define the term enzyme.
developing.a: A biological catalyst that speeds up reactions in the body.

developing.q: Name the part of the enzyme the substrate binds to.
State the optimum temperature for most human enzymes.

reaching.q: Explain why an enzyme only works on one substrate.
reaching.a: The active site has a specific shape that only one substrate is complementary to.

reaching.q: Describe what happens to an enzyme at 80 °C.
reaching.a: The active site changes shape, the enzyme denatures and can no longer bind the substrate.

reaching.q: Explain why enzyme activity is low at 5 °C.
reaching.a: Particles have little kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide less often.

mastering.q: Explain the shape of a graph of enzyme activity against temperature.
mastering.a: Activity rises to the optimum because collisions become more frequent. Above the optimum the active site denatures, so activity falls sharply to zero.

mastering.q: A student says a denatured enzyme can be cooled back down and reused. Evaluate this.
mastering.a: This is wrong. Denaturing permanently changes the shape of the active site, so cooling does not restore it.

mastering.q: Suggest why enzymes in a hot spring bacterium work at 80 °C.
mastering.a: Their enzymes have a different structure with a higher optimum temperature, so the active site does not denature at 80 °C.

reaching.q: Explain why plant cells have chloroplasts but animal cells do not.
reaching.a: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis, which happens in the chloroplasts. Animals eat their food instead.

reaching.q: What is the job of the cell wall?
reaching.a: It supports the cell and stops it bursting.

mastering.q: A cell is seen under a microscope. It has a nucleus and a cell wall. Explain what type of cell it must be.
mastering.a: It must be a plant cell, because only plant cells have a cell wall. The nucleus shows it is not a bacterium.

mastering.q: Explain why a plant wilts when it is not watered.
mastering.a: The vacuoles lose water and shrink, so the cells are no longer firm and cannot support the plant.

mastering.q: Root cells have no chloroplasts. Suggest why.
mastering.a: Roots are underground, so they get no light. Chloroplasts would be useless because photosynthesis needs light.

objectives: Recall the four factors that affect rate
Apply collision theory to unfamiliar examples
Answer exam questions under time pressure

questions.q: State the four factors that affect rate.
questions.a: Temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst.
questions.hint: Two are about the particles, two are about the conditions.

questions.q: Define activation energy.
questions.a: The minimum energy needed for a successful collision.

questions.q: How does a catalyst work?
questions.a: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
questions.hint: It does not push, it makes the hill smaller.

questions.q: What does the gradient of a rate graph show?
questions.a: The rate at that moment.

questions.q: Why does rate fall as a reaction proceeds?
questions.a: Reactants are used up, so collisions are less frequent.

questions.q: State the equation for mean rate.
questions.a: rate = quantity of product ÷ time

learn.heading: The four factors

items: Concentration: more particles in the same volume.
Surface area: more particles exposed.
Pressure (gases): particles pushed closer together.
Temperature: particles move faster AND collide harder.
Catalyst: lowers the activation energy needed.

learn.heading: Learn these three sentences
toWrite: Increasing concentration increases the frequency of collisions.
Increasing temperature increases both the frequency and the energy of collisions.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

rows.b: The rate increases because collisions are more frequent
The line gets steeper because the reaction is faster

rounds.q: Explain why powdered zinc reacts faster than a lump of zinc.
rounds.a: Larger surface area, more particles exposed, collisions are more frequent.

rounds.q: Why does a catalyst not get used up?
rounds.a: It is not a reactant. It provides a lower energy pathway and is chemically unchanged at the end.

rounds.q: A rate graph flattens after 50 s. What does this tell you?
rounds.a: The reaction has finished, one of the reactants has been completely used up.

developing.q: Name the four factors that affect rate.
State the unit of rate when gas is collected.
What is a catalyst?
developing.a: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.

reaching.q: 84 cm^3 of gas is made in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate.
Explain why concentration affects rate.
reaching.a: More particles in the same volume means collisions are more frequent, so the rate increases.

reaching.q: Explain how a catalyst increases rate.
reaching.a: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

mastering.q: Explain fully, in terms of collisions, why increasing temperature increases the rate.
mastering.a: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so collisions are more frequent. They also collide more energetically, so a greater proportion of collisions exceed the activation energy and are successful. Both effects increase the rate.

mastering.q: Compare the effect of surface area and temperature on collision energy.
mastering.a: Surface area changes only the frequency of collisions. Temperature changes both the frequency and the energy of collisions.

mastering.q: A student claims a catalyst lowers the temperature needed. Evaluate.
mastering.a: Partly right. A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the reaction can run at a lower temperature, but it does not change the temperature itself.
